newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Investors snap up Chinese banks' FRN issues.
newsitem.headline: Investors snap up Chinese banks' FRN issues.

text.p: Investors worldwide but especially in Asia are casting a covetous eye on the overseas debt issues of Chinese borrowers, bankers and traders said on Thursday.

With former investment-grade favourites South Korea and Thailand losing their appeal in the wake of banking sector malaise, China's top financial institutions are finding that their issues are in hot demand.
"The market is sick and tired of bad news out of Asia and China represents one of the positive stories," said Tony Li, director of primary markets at Chase Manhattan Bank.

Other Asian countries that are assessed as investment grade by the major rating agencies, such as Malaysia and Taiwan, are infrequent issuers, particularly in the local floating rate note market, while top-rated Singapore shuns offshore debt markets.

"There haven't been that many investment grade issuers from Asia tapping the markets so to some extent China is taking advantage of the window that has opened because of the problems in Korea and Thailand," said Avinder Bindra, managing director and head of corporate finance at Citicorp International.
China's sovereign debt is rated A3 by Moody's Investors Service and BBB by Standard and Poor's Corp.
State-owned commercial bank Bank of China on Wednesday launched a US$300 million floating rate note issue via lead managers Morgan Stanley and Bank of China International.
The notes, which mature in seven years but can be called by the issuer after five years, sold quickly, bankers said.
"We were sold out before it even launched," said a syndicate manager involved in the deal, adding that his allotment was snapped up mostly by Asian accounts.
Citibank's Bindra noted that floating rate note issues of Asian borrowers typically end up with Asian bank investors, who prefer floating paper and understand local credits.
"I would say that a small percentage, maybe 15-25 percent, gets distributed to the non-bank market (outside Asia) and to that extent people are looking at ratings and pricing," he said.
Compared with similarly rated issues from U.S. or European borrowers, Asian deals still pay a premium, although the gap has narrowed as foreign investors become familiar with the region.
Like Bank of China, China Construction Bank found eager takers for its US$200 million five-year FRN launched last week.

"The subscription was very strong," said Colin Blackwell, head of debt syndicate at lead manager Merrill Lynch Asia. He said a dearth of Chinese floating paper available in secondary markets is contributing to the popularity of new China issues.
"Over the last few years, China borrowers have tended to borrow in the Samurai or Yankee markets, with the result that Asian investors are starved of good quality PRC names," he said.

Fixed-rate bonds issued by China entities have performed extremely well in the secondary markets over the past year, and bankers suspect that many issuers, including the Ministry of Finance, may tap the international bond markets again in 1997.

But some suspect that Chinese officials are keen right now to see mainland issues launched through Hong Kong and targeted at the region's investors in order to invigorate the territory's capital markets as the handover approaches.
Hong Kong reverts to China on July 1 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Beijing's China International Trust and Investment Corp, China Investment Bank and Guangdong Infrastructure are among those entities seen setting FRN issues soon.

Up to now, China's financial institutions have tapped overseas debt markets, while corporations have raised foreign money through listing shares outside China. But bankers said they believe companies will be able to issue debt in future.
"I am optimistic that those companies that have issued H-shares will be able to go to the offshore debt markets, maybe in two or three years time," said Chase Manhattan Bank's Li.
